title: Vanity (Imitation 1.1)
hookLine: better to feel sorrow for sin than to know how to define it
tomorrow: who teaches you when the books run out?

cards: The cursor blinks under version number four. Version one was too short. Version two explained too much.
Version three quoted an article on how to apologize well. Meanwhile the friend who was hurt is still waiting, and the message is still unsent.
A small book called The Imitation of Christ, which tradition credits to a monk named Thomas à Kempis, has a first chapter that would look over your shoulder at that screen and ask one blunt question.

teach.b: Here it is, in the chapter's sense: what good does it do to argue brilliantly about the Trinity, if you lack humility and so displease the Trinity?
The book opens with Jesus in John's Gospel: "he that followeth me shall not walk in darkness." Following, it says, means copying his life, not only admiring his teaching.
Then the line that answers the versions: it would rather feel sorrow for sin than know how to define it.
Knowing the whole Bible by heart, and every saying of the philosophers, would profit nothing without the love of God and his grace.
Then it borrows from Ecclesiastes: "Vanity of vanities, saith the Preacher, vanity of vanities; all is vanity." And it adds its own exception: all is vanity, except loving God and serving him alone.
Vanity here isn't fussing in a mirror. In this chapter it means empty, something that can't hold your weight: riches that won't last, honors, wanting a long life and caring little for a good one.
Here's the thing to tell a friend tonight: the book isn't against knowing.
Its target is knowing instead of doing.
A perfect definition of sorry is a fine thing to own. Saying sorry is what reaches the other person.

how: Some Christians read The Imitation of Christ a chapter at a time as part of their daily prayer.

a sin of boasting about how much you know

s: in the Imitation, vanity mainly means caring too much about your looks
that's the popular sense. here it means empty: riches, honors, a long life that isn't a good one.
the Imitation says study and learning are worthless
its target is knowing instead of doing: learning without the love of God profits nothing.
the first chapter borrows its vanity line from Ecclesiastes
vanity of vanities, saith the Preacher. the Imitation adds an exception: loving and serving God.

games.q: your study group can explain every argument for forgiveness. one of you hasn't spoken to her brother in a year. by the Imitation's first chapter, what matters most tonight?
o: a sharper definition of forgiveness for the exam.
one of you picking up the phone to call her brother.
reading the chapter again until you all agree on it.
games.why: the chapter would rather feel sorrow for sin than know how to define it. knowing, it says, profits nothing without the love of God.

practice: Choose one good thing you already know how to do and haven't done: a message to send, a visit, a thank-you. Use the sit to settle only the first small step, and when it will happen.
If you pray, you can ask for help with that one step.

wordCard.voice: Vanity. In the Imitation, anything empty that can't bear the weight of a life; all of it, the book says, except loving and serving God.

orig.note: Latin: vanity of vanities, the line from Ecclesiastes that the Imitation borrows.

carryVoice: Your line: doing over defining. The sorrow counts for more than the right words about it. Day sixteen thirty-nine.
